item.content:encoded: US stock indexes edged higher on Friday as oil prices retreated on easing Middle East supply concerns, though telecom shares remained under pressure after SpaceX's spectrum acquisition raised competitive concerns across the sector. Oil prices fell after US President Donald Trump said on Thursday the country [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"will not attack"] Iran before US midterm elections next month, easing supply concerns. Brent crude prices were down around 1%, but were still trading over the $100-a-barrel mark. US Treasury yields were also calmer, with the benchmark 10-year yield steady at 5.25% but holding close to the 24-year high of 5.364% hit on Wednesday. The benchmark S&P 500 (.SPX) and the tech-heavy Nasdaq were headed for weekly gains despite pulling back over the previous two sessions as optimism around an AI-driven third-quarter earnings season pushed both the indexes to record highs earlier this week. The blue-chip Dow was also on track for slim weekly gains and the equal-weighted S&P 500 index (.SPXEW) was on track to snap a seven-week losing streak. Megacap growth stocks were broadly higher, with Tesla (TSLA.O) rising 1.8%, Nvidia (NVDA.O) up 1.5%, and Microsoft (MSFT.O) up 1.2%. Chip stocks were broadly higher a day after dropping sharply following [USN:L4N45U1QQ TEXT:"reports"] that OpenAI's annualized revenue was $20 billion below prior expectations. Ten out of eleven sectors advanced, with real estate (.SPLRCR) and consumer discretionary (.SPLRCD) leading the gains, each rising by about 1%. The S&P 500 communication services (.SPLRCL) was marginally lower after SpaceX (SPCX.O) gained 3.2% after the rocket and satellite maker struck a [USN:L6N45U1AK TEXT:"deal to acquire"] a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, posing a direct challenge to US wireless giants. Telecom firms traded lower, with T-Mobile US (TMUS.O) down 9.1%, AT&T (T.N) falling 7.4% and Verizon (VZ.N) easing 6.3%. At 9:42 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 136.24 points, or 0.27%, to 51,367.88, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 25.23 points, or 0.32%, to 7,790.59 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 130.99 points, or 0.48%, to 27,324.33. The quarterly earnings season gathers pace next week with big banks on deck. Optimism around strong earnings continues to support US stocks despite geopolitical and rate concerns. "The banks are great to figure out: are people borrowing, and what the situation looks like right now ... that is also going to give us data as to what the Fed may or may not do," said Kim Forrest, chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners. Among individual movers, Humana (HUM.N) jumped 16.6% after US government data showed 95% of the [USN:L4N45V0LU TEXT:"health insurer's"] members were in Medicare Advantage plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. Apple (AAPL.O) fell 2.2% after a media report that the [USN:L6N45V0A6 TEXT:"iPhone maker"] has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its newly launched iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, as soaring memory chip costs and price increases dampen consumer demand. Delta Air Lines (DAL.N) dropped 3%, as the company cut its [USN:L1N45V0AC TEXT:"annual profit forecast"] by nearly a quarter at the midpoint of the range. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.65-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.53-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 4 new 52-week highs and 3 new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 17 new highs and 75 new lows.

item.title: Eleição pode remodelar comércio entre Brasil e EUA, com foco em tarifas e minerais críticos
item.description: Duas visões drasticamente diferentes para as relações entre o Brasil e os Estados Unidos estão em jogo no segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, mas tanto as estratégias do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) quanto as do atual presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) apresentam seus próprios riscos, na avaliação de especialistas.
item.dc:creator: Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Brendan O'Boyle
item.content:encoded: Duas visões drasticamente diferentes para as relações entre o Brasil e os Estados Unidos estão em jogo no segundo turno das eleições presidenciais, mas tanto as estratégias do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) quanto as do atual presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) apresentam seus próprios riscos, na avaliação de especialistas. Flávio avançou para o segundo turno, que será realizado em 25 de outubro, com impulso após garantir 47% dos votos no primeiro turno, contra 45% de Lula, em uma campanha marcada por críticas à relação de ambos os candidatos com Washington. Quem vencer as eleições terá que lidar com as tensões entre os dois maiores parceiros comerciais do Brasil -- China e Estados Unidos -- ao mesmo tempo em que define estratégias para o desenvolvimento mineral, a industrialização e a cooperação regional. Brasil e Estados Unidos criaram um grupo de trabalho no mês passado para conduzir as negociações sobre tarifas e uma estrutura comercial bilateral mais ampla, com o acesso dos EUA aos minerais críticos e terras raras do Brasil emergindo como um ponto-chave de discórdia, enquanto Washington busca reduzir sua dependência da China para esses minerais. Caso o senador de oposição vença, "talvez os norte-americanos não queiram entregar nada para o Lula. Podem deixar tudo para o Bolsonaro", disse Rubens Barbosa, ex-embaixador brasileiro nos EUA. A estratégia de Lula em relação aos EUA tem se concentrado na defesa da soberania do Brasil, após o presidente norte-americano, Donald Trump, pressionar o Judiciário brasileiro a retirar as acusações contra o pai de Flávio, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre pena de 27 anos por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Um tom nacionalista tem norteado a atuação de Lula em relação a Washington, enquanto ele prioriza o multilateralismo e laços mais estreitos com o Sul Global, incluindo o bloco Brics de economias emergentes. Embora essa abordagem tenha contribuído para sua popularidade, Lula tem tido um progresso irregular nas negociações com Washington, disseram especialistas à Reuters. Caso Lula consiga se reeleger, o novo Congresso dominado por partidos de direita poderá pressionar um "Lula mais fraco" a mudar de tática, afirmou Monica de Bolle, pesquisadora sênior do Peterson Institute for International Economics, em Washington. "Acredito que Lula sofreria muita pressão para ceder a algumas exigências dos EUA em relação aos recursos naturais, bem como a outras questões", disse De Bolle. AS JOGADAS DE BOLSONARO Enquanto Lula tem uma "política internacional bem definida", a de Flávio é uma "página em branco", disse Rubens Ricupero, ex-diplomata brasileiro que atuou nos EUA e na Europa. O senador mantém uma relação amistosa com o governo Trump, com a ajuda de seu irmão Eduardo Bolsonaro, ex-deputado federal que reside nos EUA desde o início do ano passado e foi condenado pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal por incitar a intervenção dos EUA nos processos judiciais de seu pai em 2025. Embora nenhum dos irmãos tenha confirmado os rumores, uma pessoa próxima à campanha de Flávio disse à Reuters que os dois têm discutido possíveis funções internacionais para Eduardo, caso o senador se torne o próximo presidente do Brasil. Se Flávio for eleito presidente, "haverá uma política externa muito mais alinhada com os Estados Unidos do que o Brasil tradicionalmente tem tido", disse De Bolle. Os laços estreitos da família com o governo Trump podem garantir um ambiente de negociação mais favorável com Washington, embora Flávio corra o risco de fazer concessões em questões-chave, como minerais estratégicos, disseram especialistas. "Acho que as portas estão abertas para bons acordos entre Brasil e EUA... mas Flávio será mais cobrado a manter um discurso de independência", disse Jean Castro, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais (Abrig). Desde o lançamento de sua campanha, Flávio tem cortejado Trump, assim como outros aliados de direita no exterior, como o argentino Javier Milei e o colombiano Abelardo de la Espriella. Flávio e Trump já alinharam suas estratégias para combater o crime organizado. Em visita a Washington, em maio, o senador instou Trump a designar as principais facções criminosas brasileiras como Organizações Terroristas Estrangeiras, proposta aceita por Washington, mas rejeitada por Lula, que a considerou uma intervenção. Lula defende uma política nacional de combate ao crime organizado, com cooperação internacional. Pesquisas de opinião pública mostram que a popularidade de Lula aumentou devido às suas frequentes divergências com Trump sobre comércio e segurança, e indicam que os brasileiros responsabilizam mais Flávio pelas tarifas impostas por Trump em julho. "Ele não pode adotar uma postura que seja confundida com subserviência", disse Castro.

item.title: Canada's TSX gains after surprise job losses bolster rate-hold outlook
item.description: Canada's blue-chip stock index rose on Friday in broad-based gains as investors assessed weaker-than-expected jobs data that reinforced bets that the Bank of Canada will keep interest rates on hold at its meeting later this month.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Canada's blue-chip stock index rose on Friday in broad-based gains as investors assessed weaker-than-expected jobs data that reinforced bets that the Bank of Canada will keep interest rates on hold at its meeting later this month. The Toronto Stock Exchange's S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) was up 0.92% at 35,462.14 points by 09:46 a.m. ET (1346 GMT). Precious metal miner-linked materials sector (.GSPTTMT) rose 2.8%, leading sectorwise gains, as gold advanced more than 1% on a combination of cooling oil prices and a softer US dollar Canada's economy [USN:L1N45V0EG TEXT:"stunned widespread expectations"] to post a massive job loss in September and the unemployment rate edged up, data showed The economy lost a net of 68,300 jobs in September, while analysts polled by Reuters had forecast jobs gains of 9,200 Odds of an interest rate raise by the BoC at its next meeting dipped to 27% from 40% after the data, swap market data showed Investors still price in a 25-basis-point rate hike at its December meeting, LSEG compiled data showed The jobs report "is probably is going to tip the balance in favor of the Bank of Canada continuing to hold rates at their upcoming meetings rather than raising them," said Brian Madden, chief investment officer with First Avenue Investment Counsel Aritzia (ATZ.TO) shares surged 16.7% after the apparel retailer topped analyst expectations for second-quarter revenue and profit, lifting the consumer discretionary sector (.GSPTTCD) 2.1% higher Eight out of 10 major sectors were trading higher, while energy (.SPTTEN) gained 1.1%, despite softer oil prices, and heavily weighted financials (.SPTTFS) inched 0.3% higher Despite the session's gains, the TSX remained on track for a third straight weekly decline as elevated bond yields and inflationary worries pressured risk appetite

item.title: French student protesters vow to keep up their fight after scoring first win
item.description: The protests have snowballed into a wider movement, with more university students weighing in to express their anger over what they call a dysfunctional system.
item.dc:creator: Makini Brice, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: French student unions vowed on Friday to keep up protests after scoring what they called their first win in a campaign that is increasingly supported by Paris' elite universities, with 141 schools still shut around the country. The protests have snowballed into a wider movement, with more university students weighing in to express their anger over what they call a dysfunctional system, worsened by spending cuts spurred by France's budget crunch. Student and teacher unions have called for another round of nationwide school strikes next Tuesday. France's education ministry is in the process of urgently contacting around 3,000 spare teachers who could be sent to schools with the most pressing needs, often located in low-income areas, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said. Speaking during a visit to a school in the Paris region that was vandalised during protests, he said more than 100 teaching staff had been injured so far in the nationwide protests. The movement has fueled similar student protests in Belgium, which on Friday were amplified by a national strike during which scuffles broke out between protesters and police in Brussels. ELITE UNIVERSITIES ARE WEIGHING IN Police cleared a blockade at Assas university, a top French law school in central Paris, on Friday morning. Nearby, elite engineering school Mines Paris was also disrupted by blockades. The Institut Catholique, a private university known for being particularly conservative, said on its website it would switch to remote classes due to a blockade of its campus. Student unions meanwhile hailed what they see as their first real win, after the government late on Thursday pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are fully qualified but have not yet started work, to fill staffing gaps, one of the protesters' main grievances. The move, which the government called an "emergency plan", shows it is worthwhile for students to continue their protests, Marius Mesnil, from a high school student union, told Franceinfo radio. "I find it crazy we need to block hundreds of high schools just to get a vacancy plan," he added. The measure is effective immediately and will cost "several dozen million euros", Geffray told broadcaster TF1 late on Thursday. MARKETS MONITORING GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO PROTESTS Three weeks into the protest, President Emmanuel Macron's government is struggling to work out how to balance demands for more education spending with the need to rein in public debt. Investors are closely watching the government's next moves in a highly indebted country where street anger has often been tamed with more state spending. This time, France's large pension outlays and its need to rein in public spending leave little room for manoeuvre. Stephane Boujnah, the head of Euronext, which runs the Paris stock market, said Paris urgently needed to make tough choices. "What sacrifice are we asking of our own children? ... maybe we need to spend a little less on pensions so that we have a little more money for the children," he told RMC radio. Nearly 10% of teaching hours are unstaffed at French state high schools, according to education ministry figures, prompting a growing number of wealthier parents to abandon the public sector in [USN:L1N45U0DV TEXT:"favour of private schooling"], a trend that some experts say will only reinforce social inequality. "Let's be frank, families are leaving public schools for our institutions," said Pierre-Vincent Gueret, who heads France's federation of Catholic private schools. The interior ministry said [USN:L1N45U08J TEXT:"71,500 people"] took to the streets in Paris and elsewhere on Thursday. While most protests were peaceful, violence flared up in some places. In Belgium, meanwhile, students joined demonstrations alongside striking workers as the country's two largest labour unions staged a national strike on Friday, disrupting public transport, air travel and other sectors. Thousands of people marched through central Brussels in a protest that was largely peaceful, although some scuffles broke out with police, who used tear gas and water cannons in some instances. One banner carried by student protesters read: "I skipped class to defend class."

item.title: Nobel/Paix-L'ancienne juge de la CPI Navanethem "Navi" Pillay remporte le prix Nobel de la paix 2026
item.description: Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, ancienne juge de la Cour pénale internationale (CPI), qui a supervisé une enquête de l'Onu ayant conclu qu’Israël avait commis un génocide à Gaza, a remporté vendredi le prix Nobel de la paix pour "ses efforts en faveur de la paix et du droit international".
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, ancienne juge de la Cour pénale internationale (CPI), qui a supervisé une enquête de l'Onu ayant conclu qu’Israël avait commis un génocide à Gaza, a remporté vendredi le prix Nobel de la paix pour "ses efforts en faveur de la paix et du droit international". En décernant le prix à Navi Pillay, âgée de 85 ans et qui a siégé dans plusieurs juridictions internationales, notamment au Tribunal pénal international pour le Rwanda (TPIR), le Comité Nobel a souligné l'importance du maintien d'un ordre international fondé sur le droit. La Cour pénale internationale (CPI), dont le siège est à La Haye, est depuis longtemps la cible du président américain Donald Trump, dont la campagne contre la Cour s'est intensifiée après l'émission, l'année dernière, de mandats d'arrêt contre le Premier ministre israélien Benjamin Netanyahu et son ancien ministre de la Défense. "Le système du droit international est soumis à une pression considérable et ses institutions sont attaquées", a déclaré le comité Nobel. "Nous assistons à un glissement vers une politique fondée sur les rapports de force, au détriment des cadres juridiques et du respect du droit et de la justice à l'échelle mondiale. Chaque fois que la force l'emporte sur le droit, la stabilité, la confiance et la coexistence pacifique sont fragilisées." Le comité Nobel n'a mentionné ni Donald Trump ni Israël dans son communiqué. Navi Pillay a présidé la commission d'enquête de l'Onu sur Gaza, qui a conclu l'année dernière qu'Israël avait commis un [USN:L5N3V308F TEXT:"génocide"] à territoire palestinien occupé. Israël avait alors rejeté ce rapport, le qualifiant de "scandaleux" et de "faux". Israël a d'ailleurs dénoncé l'attribution du prix Nobel de la paix à Navi Pillay. À NUREMBERG AU MOMENT DE L’ANNONCE Elle a appris la nouvelle alors qu’elle participait à une conférence juridique dans le bâtiment de Nuremberg, en Allemagne, où le premier tribunal pénal international a été créé en 1945-1946 pour juger les crimes nazis. "La dernière chose que j’ai faite, c’est remettre le rapport sur Gaza, dans lequel je qualifie de génocide ce qui s’y passe", a déclaré Navi Pillay devant un public rassemblé pour célébrer cette distinction, selon une vidéo publiée sur les réseaux sociaux par le directeur d'Amnesty International. "Si vous applaudissez un peu plus fort, je partagerai peut-être ce prix avec Trump", a-t-elle ajouté, déclenchant des rires. Elle faisait apparemment référence à la décision de la lauréate de l'an dernier, [USN:L5N3VR0DQ TEXT:"Maria Corina Machado"], de remettre sa médaille Nobel au président américain en janvier afin d’obtenir son soutien à sa campagne pour une transition démocratique au Venezuela. Navi Pillay a averti que les attaques politiques croissantes contre le droit international risquaient de ramener le monde à un système dans lequel "c’est la force plutôt que le droit qui détermine quelles souffrances comptent". "Cette distinction renforce ma conviction que nous devons nous unir pour défendre l’État de droit, défendre l’indépendance des tribunaux et défendre un ordre juridique international fondé sur des principes", a déclaré Navi Pillay dans un communiqué. LE DROIT SOUS PRESSION L'organisme chargé de décerner le prix voulait rappeler au monde que l’État de droit constituait le fondement du système international mis en place pour garantir la paix et que ce système était soumis à de "très fortes pressions", a déclaré son président. "Bien entendu, les États les plus puissants ont une responsabilité particulière, mais, malheureusement, nous observons ce phénomène partout dans le monde", a déclaré Joergen Watne Frydnes à Reuters. "Les institutions sont attaquées. De nombreux juges font l’objet de sanctions", a-t-il ajouté. La présidente de la Cour pénale internationale (CPI), Tomoko Akane, a salué cette distinction. "À l’heure où l’ordre juridique international et l’État de droit sont confrontés à de profonds défis, cette reconnaissance revêt une importance particulière", a-t-elle déclaré dans un communiqué. Le mois dernier, Donald Trump a appelé les pays à quitter la CPI. Il a imposé des sanctions ciblées à plusieurs procureurs et juges de la Cour et, selon des sources, envisage des sanctions plus larges en représailles aux poursuites visant des dirigeants israéliens. Haakon Gjerloew, directeur par intérim de l’Institut de recherche sur la paix d’Oslo, a toutefois estimé que le comité Nobel ne critiquait pas directement Donald Trump en récompensant Navi Pillay. "Je pense qu’il s'agit plutôt, de manière générale, de promouvoir un ordre international fondé sur le droit. Bien entendu, il pourrait réagir au fait qu’une personne ayant travaillé au sein de la CPI soit récompensée, mais ce n’est pas une attaque directe contre Trump", a déclaré Haakon Gjerloew. "UNE BOUSSOLE MORALE À TOUTE ÉPREUVE" Née à Durban, dans la province sud-africaine du Natal, au sein d’une famille d’origine tamoule indienne, Navi Pillay a été Haut-Commissaire des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme de 2008 à 2014. En 1967, elle est devenue la première femme à ouvrir un cabinet d’avocats dans le Natal et la première femme non blanche à siéger à la Haute Cour d’Afrique du Sud. Elle est la cinquième personnalité sud-africaine à recevoir le prix Nobel de la paix, après Nelson Mandela et Frederik Willem de Klerk, l’archevêque Desmond Tutu et Albert Luthuli. Le bureau du président sud-africain Cyril Ramaphosa a salué cette distinction dans un communiqué: "Le président Ramaphosa salue la reconnaissance accordée à la juge Pillay par le Comité Nobel norvégien, qui constitue un hommage profond au courage, à l’intégrité et à l’engagement de toute une vie en faveur de la justice de cette juriste chevronnée". Tout au long de sa longue carrière, Navi Pillay a demandé des comptes aux États et aux dirigeants nationaux, redonné espoir aux victimes de violences et de conflits et fait preuve d’une boussole morale inébranlable, a déclaré le comité Nobel. "Un fil conducteur relie ses premiers engagements, lorsqu’elle défendait Nelson Mandela et d’autres opposants à l’apartheid, à son travail de juge dans certaines des affaires judiciaires internationales les plus importantes de notre époque", indique le communiqué. Navi Pillay continue d’exercer des fonctions judiciaires. Elle siège actuellement à la Cour internationale de Justice (CIJ). L'ONU SALUE UNE DISTINCTION EN FAVEUR DES DROITS HUMAINS "C'est une excellente nouvelle, nous avons besoin de davantage de dévouement et d'engagement en faveur des droits humains", a déclaré aux journalistes à Genève Shabia Mantoo, porte-parole du Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l'homme . "Nous espérons que cette distinction encouragera et continuera d'encourager et d'inspirer d'autres personnes à prendre la parole pour défendre et promouvoir les droits humains de tous, partout dans le monde", a-t-elle ajouté. UNE TRADITION DEPUIS 1901 Le prix Nobel de la paix est le cinquième annoncé cette année, conformément à la tradition, après ceux de [USN:L8N45R0OX TEXT:"médecine"] lundi, de [USN:L8N45S0NZ TEXT:"physique"] mardi, de [USN:L8N45T0LN TEXT:"chimie"] mercredi et de [USN:L8N45U0W3 TEXT:"littérature"] jeudi. Le prix Nobel de l'économie sera annoncé lundi prochain. Décernés depuis 1901, à quelques interruptions près, principalement pendant les Première et Seconde Guerres mondiales, [USN:L8N45T231 TEXT:"les prix Nobel"] comptent une sixième catégorie, celle de l’économie, créée en 1968 par la banque centrale suédoise, la Riksbank. Doté de 12 millions de couronnes suédoises (1,07 million d'euros), le prix Nobel de la paix sera remis à l’hôtel de ville d’Oslo le 10 décembre, date anniversaire de la mort d’Alfred Nobel, inventeur et industriel suédois dont la fortune provenait notamment de l'invention de la dynamite. L'an dernier, le prix avait été décerné à la dirigeante de l’opposition vénézuélienne [USN:L5N3VR0DQ TEXT:"Maria Corina Machado"] pour son action en faveur de la démocratie au Venezuela.

item.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: Navi Pillay, who oversaw a UN report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won "for her efforts to promote peace and international law".
item.dc:creator: Gwladys Fouche, Nora Buli
item.content:encoded: Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law". Giving the prize to Pillay, 85, who has been a judge on several international courts, including the International Criminal Court and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, underlined the importance of maintaining an organised international order, the Nobel committee said in its citation. The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of US President Donald Trump, whose [USN:L6N45G1BM TEXT:"campaign against it has escalated"] since the court announced arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister last year. "The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack," the Nobel committee said. "We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence." The Nobel committee's citation made no reference to Trump, nor Israel. Pillay was also chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that [USN:L2N3V306V TEXT:"concluded last year"] that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report at the time as "scandalous". Israel condemned the award. "The decision of the Nobel committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of antisemitism like Pillay herself," the Israeli ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron, told Reuters. "As the chair of the Commission of Inquiry she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence. Campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda." IN NUREMBERG AT TIME OF ANNOUNCEMENT Pillay received news of the award while she was attending a legal conference in the building in Nuremberg, Germany, where the first international criminal tribunal was set up in 1945-1946 to judge the crimes of the Nazis, 80 years and nine days after the verdicts in those trials were delivered. "The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," Pillay told a crowd gathering to celebrate the award, a video posted on social media by the head of rights group Amnesty International showed. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she added, to laughter, in an apparent reference to the decision by last year's laureate, Maria Corina Machado, to give her Nobel medal to the US president in January to help gain support for her campaign for a democratic Venezuela. Trump has repeatedly said he deserved to win the Nobel Peace Prize. [USN:L8N45V108 TEXT:"Pillay later dedicated"] the award to "all the survivors of international crimes as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign". Turning her attention to world leaders, she told them: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war". 'INSTITUTIONS ARE UNDER ATTACK' The award body wanted the world to remember that the rule of law underpinned the international system set up to ensure peace and that this system was under "tremendous pressure", its chair said. "Of course, the most powerful states have particular responsibility, but we see it all over the world, unfortunately," Joergen Watne Frydnes told Reuters. "The institutions are under attack. Many judges are being sanctioned." The award was welcomed by ICC President Tomoko Akane. "At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance," she said in a statement. Trump last month urged countries to leave the ICC, has [USN:L6N3Z200M TEXT:"imposed targeted sanctions"] on several prosecutors and judges at the court and, according to sources, is considering [USN:L1N45C05S TEXT:"wider sanctions"] in retaliation for the targeting of Israeli leaders. Still, Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said the Nobel committee was not directly criticising Trump by rewarding Pillay. "I think it's generally rather a promotion of an international legal world order. Of course, he might react to someone who has been part of the ICC, but it's not a direct attack on Trump," Gjerloew said. 'FIRM MORAL COMPASS' Born in Durban, in South Africa's Natal province, into a family of Indian Tamil origin, Pillay served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. In 1967 she became the first woman to start a law practice in Natal and, after the end of apartheid, the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court. She was the fifth South African national to win the Nobel Peace Prize, after Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk, Archbishop Desmond Tutu and Albert Luthuli. Pillay held states and national leaders accountable and demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career, said the committee. "A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," said the citation. Pillay continues to work as a judge, currently serving on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide, the citation said. The peace prize is the fifth Nobel awarded this week, after [USN:L1N45U0CQ TEXT:"literature"], [USN:L1N45T09K TEXT:"chemistry"], [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"physics"] and [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"medicine"]. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado won in [USN:L2N3VR066 TEXT:"2025"]. The Nobel Peace Prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.

item.title: Moyes surprised Everton owners are open to sale of controlling stake
item.description: Everton manager David Moyes said on Friday he was surprised by The Friedkin Group's decision to consider selling a controlling stake in the Premier League club, less than two years after the US-based outfit took over.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Everton manager David Moyes said on Friday he was surprised by The Friedkin Group's decision to consider selling a controlling stake in the Premier League club, less than two years after the US-based outfit took over. TFG said earlier on Friday it was open to selling a controlling stake as part of efforts to attract fresh investment, less than two years after it acquired Everton from former owner Farhad Moshiri in December 2024. "I truly believed with new ownership we were in it completely," Moyes told reporters ahead of Everton's Premier League game at Hull City on Sunday. "My ambition coming back was trying to get Everton back to the levels they have been in the past and that is challenging for Europe more often. "It has been a difficult summer for us. I only found out this morning. Maybe I am a little bit surprised, but maybe I shouldn't be that surprised." Everton are seventh in the table after five games. TFG took control of a club grappling with financial difficulties and a prolonged period of instability and has since overseen Everton's move into the Hill Dickinson Stadium while working to improve their financial position. "When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch," the owners said in a statement. The group said its immediate priority had been to provide the stability, investment and support required to secure Everton's future, including completing the new stadium. "With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton," TFG said. TFG added that it would only consider proposals from parties it believed could build on the progress made since its takeover and added that it would continue to support the club on and off the pitch throughout the process. TFG's decision follows a transfer window that, according to British media, [USN:L6N44U0S9 TEXT:"drew criticism from supporters"]. Everton generated significant income through player sales but made only limited additions to their squad before the deadline. TFG, which also owns Italian club AS Roma and French side AS Cannes, said it had retained investment bank Moelis & Company to advise on the process. The group and Everton said they would make no further comment while the process was under way.

item.title: Poland's 'Bloody Friday' school threats prompt huge police operation
item.description: Thousands of Polish police officers visited schools nationwide on Friday in an effort to reassure pupils after two teenage stabbing sprees in as many days sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of attacks.
item.dc:creator: Pawel Florkiewicz, Alicja Surdy
item.content:encoded: Thousands of Polish police officers visited schools nationwide on Friday in an effort to reassure pupils after two teenage stabbing sprees in as many days sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of attacks. Social media in Poland has been filled with talk of a supposed online challenge that could be behind the attacks and which would end with a bloodbath at schools on Friday, but police said their investigations had found no evidence of this. By midday, 24,000 police officers had been deployed to 15,000 schools and 19 young people had been detained, mainly for making threats online, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said. "There will be no compromise here - the safety of youngsters is the most important thing," he told a press conference. Education Minister Barbara Nowacka said 59 schools around the country were closed, mainly in the Mazowsze region where this week's attacks took place. On Thursday, a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera [USN:L8N45U0GO TEXT:"killed one employee"] and injured two others at a Polish primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of Warsaw. On Wednesday, a 19-year-old [USN:L1N45T0N9 TEXT:"wounded 10 people"] including himself at another school in Ostroleka, north of the capital. The scale of the police deployment and the school closures underscored the shock caused by two attacks in a country where school stabbings have been very rare, and the speed with which online rumours amplified the fear. ONLINE THREATS AND DISINFORMATION SOW TERROR In Ostroleka, schools were operating as normal but attendance was just 25%, the PAP state news agency quoted Mayor Pawel Niewiadomski as saying. In Warsaw, 59-year-old NGO manager and mother-of-four Dorota Czekaj told Reuters the week's events had left her "simply terrified". She called for a tough response to online content that could encourage violence. "Unlimited access to all sorts of content, some of it very negative, certainly affects... our brains and contributes to a general social desensitisation in some way," she said. "And I think we simply have to respond to this more firmly." Authorities warned people of the risks of online disinformation, with Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz suggesting Russia could use such events to sow panic. Russia has repeatedly denied attempting to destabilise Western countries using online disinformation. Polish police made a string of arrests on Friday. These included a 13-year-old from Warsaw who posted a photo of a knife in a class group chat and threatened other students, a 14-year-old in Warsaw detained on school grounds with a knife and firecrackers, and two 15-year-olds from Pruszkow County just outside the capital who posted a video with threats to kill. Several social media accounts posted pictures on Thursday of a TikTok account which supposedly belonged to the attacker from Leszczydol-Nowiny and featured images taken just before the incident. Reuters was unable to find the account, which appeared to have been taken down. "Officers from the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC) are aware of the content posted on the TikTok account in question," CBZC told Reuters by email, adding that the platform was cooperating with the agency. TikTok did not reply to an emailed request for comment.

item.title: India to deploy thousands of security forces in Delhi for protest over poll chief
item.description: Authorities in India's capital Delhi are deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel ahead of a protest called for Saturday by the "Cockroach" youth movement to demand the elections chief quit over a revision of voter lists.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma, Sarita Singh, Rajesh Kr Singh
item.content:encoded: Authorities in India's capital Delhi are deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel ahead of a protest called for Saturday by the "Cockroach" youth movement to demand the elections chief quit over a [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"revision of voter lists"]. Several long-distance trains coming into Delhi were also cancelled on Friday, and 57 metro stations were closed from Friday night, authorities said after organisers said they were expecting thousands of people to join the protest. The anger against the voter verification drive that began last year has become one of the biggest political controversies since Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, and comes ahead of crucial state elections starting early next year. Election Commission data, which is also cited by BJP, shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from voter lists during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced, and 28 million who were dead. YOUTH 'NO LONGER SCARED', COCKROACH MOVEMENT SAYS Opposition parties say the voter deletions affected the outcome of some recent state elections that Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won, and have cast a shadow on the electoral process in the world's largest democracy. The BJP says Modi's popularity and India's economic growth are some key reasons for its electoral dominance. Thousands of police and paramilitary forces, including some from sensitive areas such as Indian Kashmir, were being sent into the capital for the protest, according to a government document seen by Reuters. However, the Cockroach movement remained defiant. "The youth of this country are no longer scared of you," founder Abhijeet Dipke said in a post on X, addressing Modi ahead of the protests. The self-named "Cockroach Janta Party", a youth movement that began as an online satire, said it wanted Chief Election Commissioner [USN:L4N45K0DB TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar to resign"], echoing demands by the opposition parties which have been protesting almost daily since last week. The CJP gained popularity this year after its weeks-long agitation against exam paper leaks [USN:L1N43R02E TEXT:"culminated in the resignation"] of the education minister, dealing Modi his biggest political setback in years. SEVEN STATES DUE TO VOTE IN 2027 The BJP and the commission deny allegations of election manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately impacted by the deletions. At least seven Indian states are due to hold elections in 2027, including Uttar Pradesh ruled by the BJP. The state is India's most populous and is considered a bellwether in national politics. Parliamentary polls are not due until 2029. India, with at least 960 million eligible voters in 2024, began the [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"verification"] effort last year ahead of elections in the eastern state of Bihar and has now covered the majority of states. Police in the capital said the CJP did not have permission for Saturday's protest and could face legal action if protesters violated rules. The CJP said police in several states were detaining thousands of its supporters as they headed to Saturday's protest.

item.title: BASF considers raising offer for Evonik, sources say
item.description: Chemicals maker BASF , facing intense competition from China, could raise its offer for Evonik if there are talks with the specialty chemicals maker, two people close to BASF told Reuters on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Inverardi
item.content:encoded: Chemicals maker BASF (BASFn.DE) , facing intense competition from China, could raise its offer for Evonik (EVKn.DE) if there are talks with the specialty chemicals maker, two people close to BASF told Reuters on Friday. Evonik said in September that BASF, one of the world's largest chemicals makers, had approached it over a possible takeover, but added that no [USN:L8N45H0MN TEXT:"talks"] were currently taking place. People close to the negotiations later said Evonik had [USN:L6N45K0R8 TEXT:"rejected"] the bid of €10.3 billion ($11.7 billion), or €22.15 per share, as too low. "It is safe to assume that the current offer is not the final word," one of the people close to BASF said. Shares in Evonik were up 1.7% to €21.34 at 1328 GMT on Friday having risen as much as 2.7% against Thursday's close. A spokesperson for Evonik's largest shareholder, the RAG Foundation, said that the board of trustees was briefed by the executive board of RAG Foundation on BASF's interest in acquiring Evonik, but declined to give further details. A BASF spokesperson declined to comment. Evonik reiterated that no talks were currently underway. REGIONAL STATE COULD PLAY KEY ROLE BASF was also considering commitments to Evonik employees, the people said. The German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where Evonik is based, said on Monday that jobs at Evonik and its independent development must not be jeopardised by a takeover. The state could have significant influence because state premier Hendrik Wuest sits on the board of trustees of RAG Foundation. Any sale of the foundation's shares would require the board's approval. BASF, which makes engineering plastics, super-absorbent polymers, vitamins and chemicals for industrial uses, is at risk of losing its top global ranking by chemicals revenue to China's Sinopec (600028.SS) , whose chemicals division revenue was broadly neck and neck with BASF's group revenue of €59.7 billion last year. Evonik's portfolio, which includes high-tech plastics and feed additives as well as ingredients for coatings and household products, would offer possible cost benefits through synergies with BASF, a BASF company source said last month.

item.title: Australia fight back in first test before bad light ends opening day's play
item.description: Australia's captain Pat Cummins and Matt Renshaw led an afternoon fightback to see the tourists to 187-6 before bad light brought a premature halt to play on the opening day of the first test against South Africa on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gleeson
item.content:encoded: Australia's captain Pat Cummins and Matt Renshaw led an afternoon fightback to see the tourists to 187-6 before bad light brought a premature halt to play on the opening day of the first test against South Africa on Friday. The pair put on an unbeaten 63 for the seventh wicket with Renshaw four runs short of a fifty and Cummins 33 not out. The umpires took the players off one hour before the scheduled close as windy and gloomy conditions coincided with South Africa bringing back the pacy Anrich Nortje into the attack and when he sent a bouncer over Renshaw’s head, play was immediately halted after the light meters were consulted. The umpires waited out in the middle for another 45 minutes before calling off the day's proceedings. Nortje was returning after almost four years away from first-class cricket, and took two wickets in the space of three balls before tea to give the hosts the upper hand. The 32-year-old had not played since March 2023 as persistent injury and a focus on the T20 format kept him away from red-ball cricket but he justified his recall with a fiery spell after lunch that left the tourists teetering. South Africa captain Temba Bavuma predicted Nortje could provide “X-factor”, and he did as much in having Alex Carey caught at second slip off a fuller delivery that clocked in at 143 kph and then, two balls later, snagging Beau Webster caught behind to see Australia fall to 124-6. The fortunes of Nortje, who finished the day with 2-40 off 13.2 overs, contrasted with those of Australian cancer survivor Nic Maddinson, also making a comeback, but who failed to get a run. The 34-year-old, a surprise choice to open after Australia won the toss and chose to bat, survived 33 balls without scoring before Marco Jansen bowled him to end a remarkable return following his battle with cancer last year. His duck was the longest by an Australian opener in test history and the third-longest by any test opener. It was Maddinson’s first test appearance in almost a decade, having not played first-class cricket for 18 months as he fought testicular cancer that had spread to his lungs. He was only named in the team half an hour before play started Australia counter-attacked after Travis Head (9) and Maddinson went early, with Marnus Labuschagne and Steve Smith putting together a 60-run partnership for the third wicket before Wiaan Mulder (2-31) trapped Labuschagne lbw for 37 with the last ball before lunch. Smith scored 25 on his first test appearance in South Africa since the 2018 tour that led to his one-year ban for his role in the ball-tampering scandal known as "[USN:L6N45T0FP TEXT:"Sandpapergate"]". Smith walked to the crease without any noticeable heckling from the sparse crowd and quickly set about speeding up the scoring, with two sixes when spinner Keshav Maharaj was introduced to the home attack. However, Smith was dismissed in the first over after lunch, getting a thick edge to gully to earn Jansen (2-35) a second wicket.

item.title: Europe Inc heads for another quarter of strong profits, defying global gloom
item.description: Major European companies are expected to report substantially higher third-quarter earnings, defying a challenging backdrop in global markets as borrowing costs in some of the world's biggest economies hover near multi-year highs.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Major European companies are expected to report substantially higher third-quarter earnings, defying a challenging backdrop in [USN:L1N45V0AO TEXT:"global markets"] as borrowing costs in some of the world's biggest economies hover near multi-year highs. Companies on Europe's benchmark STOXX 600 index (.STOXX) are expected to report quarterly earnings growth of 21% on aggregate, mostly buoyed by the energy and basic materials sectors, the latest LSEG I/B/E/S data showed on Thursday. That is slightly lower than the second quarter's 23.9% growth but would mark the second-best quarterly profit growth in the past 16 quarters. Excluding the energy sector, the expected growth rate for STOXX 600 companies is a more modest 9.7%. Revenues of European blue-chip companies are seen increasing by 10.6% from a year ago, also above the average of the past couple of years. "Demand is strong enough to allow companies to pass on higher prices which leads to higher sales. At the same time, energy costs make up a smaller share of sales than headlines would suggest," a Deutsche Bank report said earlier this week. European energy majors have been benefiting from the consequences of the US-Israeli war with Iran and from Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries, which have [USN:L6N4580TA TEXT:"sharply cut exports"] from some of the world's biggest producers of fossil fuels. They are now expected to post profit growth of 115.9% for the third quarter, according to the LSEG report. Meanwhile, companies in the European real estate sector are seen delivering earnings 71.5% smaller than in the same period last year. Next week, investors will be closely looking at results of chip equipment supplier ASML (ASML.AS) , Europe's most valuable listed company, and Swedish telecoms equipment maker Ericsson (ERICb.ST) to assess the tone of the earnings season.

item.title: Take Five: Bangkok blues
item.description: The IMF-World Bank meetings take place in Bangkok against a backdrop of high energy costs and rising central bank rates, while the latest US and China data, Wall Street earnings and turbulent bond markets point to a packed week ahead.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The IMF-World Bank meetings take place in Bangkok against a backdrop of high energy costs and rising central bank rates, while the latest US and China data, Wall Street earnings and turbulent bond markets point to a packed week ahead. Here's all you need to know about what's coming up in financial markets by Tatiana Bautzer and Lewis Krauskopf in New York, Rocky Swift in Tokyo, and Marc Jones and Dhara Ranasinghe in London. 1/ IMF'S ASIA GETAWAY The IMF and World Bank annual meetings go on tour to Bangkok next week with three themes front and centre: growth, debt and geopolitics. Market focus is on Tuesday's updated IMF [USN:L6N45T0FB TEXT:"World Economic Outlook"] given the Iran war has already forced two cuts to its global GDP forecast this year. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has signalled it won't make easy reading given sky-high energy prices, record public debt and tetchy bond markets. Fractured and fractious geopolitics, including conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine , will feature prominently, as will how to regulate AI given an arms race between the US and China. Senegal's recently announced [USN:L8N45S13U TEXT:"debt rework plan"] is likely to get attention from IMF crisis watchers too, although they will have more than half an eye on whether [USN:L8N45S0RJ TEXT:"France"] is dragging the euro zone back in that direction as well. 2/ A TEST FOR RATE BETS A fresh look at US inflation on Wednesday will be among the last key data released before the [USN:L6N4570XW TEXT:"Federal Reserve"] decides whether to hike interest rates again to contain high prices. The September consumer price index is set to show a 0.6% rise on a monthly basis. The core measure, excluding volatile energy and food components, is estimated to increase just 0.2%, according to a Reuters poll. Thursday's producer price numbers will further flesh out the inflation picture. Retail sales data is also out that day. Core CPI for August rose at its [USN:L1N452123 TEXT:"fastest pace in four months"], helping cement the Fed's first rate hike since 2023. Bets on another hike when the Fed meets in late October have fallen back. A hot CPI report could change that. 3/ WHICH WAY TO WALL STREET? It's the start of the Q3 US earnings season and who better to kick things off than the [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"banks"]? Four of the six largest US lenders, JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , [USN:L4N45K1NY TEXT:"Goldman Sachs"] (GS.N) , Citigroup (C.N) and Wells Fargo (WFC.N) , report on Tuesday, followed a day after by Morgan Stanley (MS.N) and Bank of America (BAC.N) . Earnings are expected to rise up to 20% relative to last year. Still, the surge in Treasury yields to multi-decade highs has hurt shares - the KBW Bank Index is down around 13% from its peak in August. Investors will be looking for signs that the recent spike in government borrowing costs may curb dealmaking and lending growth, as well as pressure funding costs across the industry. 4/ MADE IN CHINA Chinese data on Wednesday will show whether AI-related exports are still propping up an economy [USN:L1N44I01C TEXT:"hobbled"] by anaemic demand at home. Overseas shipments from the world's second-largest economy have logged double-digit growth for four straight months on surging global [USN:L6N45004F TEXT:"demand"] for AI goods, electric vehicles, solar cells and lithium-ion batteries. But a prolonged property slump has kept domestic consumption in the [USN:L1N44E058 TEXT:"doldrums"]. Exports are forecast to have jumped 25.3% year-on-year in September in dollar terms, according to a Reuters poll, up from 25% in August. Imports are projected to show 23.5% growth versus 28.2% previously. Separate figures the same day are expected to show continuing [USN:L1N45101J TEXT:"price pressures"] related to the Iran war. The producer price index is forecast to have risen to 4.4% in September from 3.8% the previous period, while consumer inflation may have edged up to 1.1% from 0.8%. 5/ TO CATCH A FALLING KNIFE Surging government borrowing costs are clearly luring some investors back to bonds as evidenced by the strong demand at the latest [USN:L1N45T0QB TEXT:"US"] and [USN:L6N45U06X TEXT:"Japanese auctions"]. But do you really want to catch a falling knife? That's the question for traders in the coming week as the bond selloff shows few signs of abating. US and French bond yields have hit fresh 24-year highs and market volatility is high. The French-German 10-year bond yield spread, at around 136 basis points, was below 100 bps a month ago. The [USN:L8N45S0RJ TEXT:"speed and scale of the rise"] in the French risk premium is hurting Italian peers, the [USN:L6N45S0D2 TEXT:"euro"] and European shares. It's also led to some finger-pointing at the role of [USN:L8N45O0S7 TEXT:"hedge funds"] - that fast-money group that has stepped up its presence in systemically important bond markets of late.

item.title: Oil falls as Trump comments on Iran talks ease supply concerns
item.description: Oil fell on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before midterm elections next month and talked of "productive" talks to end their war that has disrupted global energy markets.
item.dc:creator: Seher Dareen
item.content:encoded: Oil fell on Friday as Middle East supply concerns eased after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before midterm elections next month and talked of "productive" talks to end their war that has disrupted global energy markets. Plans by China, the world's top oil importer, to [USN:L1N45V02I TEXT:"resume refined fuel exports"] after a brief halt during its Golden Week holiday, also weighed on the market. Reuters reported the development on Friday, citing sources. Brent crude futures dropped $1.10, or 1.1%, to $103.18 a barrel by 1328 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures fell 49 cents or 0.5% to $91.00. On a weekly basis, Brent prices are set to rise after settling 4% higher on Thursday, while WTI is set for a slight decline. Trump's Iran pledge along with China's resumption of product exports were moving prices lower, said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga. Prices have been volatile this week as threats to shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20% of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased in October. On Thursday, Trump said Washington was having "productive discussions" with Iran and said [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"no attack"] was planned before the November 3 midterm congressional elections after media reports that he was considering an attack before then. Iran's Tasnim news agency reported the same day that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Tehran is reviewing the US response to its proposal that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. The US is still pressuring Iran economically to try to end the war, now in its eighth month, imposing sanctions targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals. The Iran war and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have disrupted supplies of refined fuels such as gasoline, jet fuel and especially diesel fuel. The oil market is also contending with [USN:L1N45U0RS TEXT:"Hurricane Isaias"] in the Gulf of Mexico where producers have shut in about 1.3 million barrels per day, or 62.9%, of current oil production as of Thursday, according to the US Marine Minerals Administration.

item.title: Gold hits one-week high on softer oil prices
item.description: Gold rose to a one-week high on Friday, as falling oil prices eased concerns around inflation and pressure on US Treasuries, while traders assessed the likelihood of further US Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Sinha
item.content:encoded: Gold rose to a one-week high on Friday, as falling oil prices eased concerns around inflation and pressure on US Treasuries, while traders assessed the likelihood of further US Federal Reserve interest rate hikes. Spot gold rose 1.3% to $4,186.04 by 09:39 a.m. EDT (1339 GMT), heading for a weekly gain of about 1%. The metal fell to a two-month low on Wednesday as a stronger dollar and rising US Treasury yields weighed on the non-yielding metal. US gold futures for December delivery also added 1.3%, trading at $4,211.20 per ounce. "Bullion is finding some breathing room today as oil benchmarks and longer-term Treasury yields ease away from recent highs," said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit. Oil prices fell as worries over Middle East supply disruptions subsided after US President Donald Trump said the country would not attack Iran before the US midterm elections next month. US 10-year Treasury yields were off over two-decade highs hit on Wednesday. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said on Thursday the US central bank [USN:L6N45U16W TEXT:"will need to hike rates again to bring inflation back to its 2% target"]. Traders are pricing in a 19% chance of a rate hike in October and an 84% probability of at least one 25-basis-point increase by December, according to the CME's FedWatch tool. Gold tends to lose its appeal compared to yield-bearing assets in a high interest-rate environment. "It is arguable that a further Fed hike is already priced in but so is the expectation for continued official sector net purchases," said Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis at Stone X. "Without any Black Swan event I find it hard to see gold breaking convincingly higher." Meanwhile, [USN:L4N45V08X TEXT:"gold demand in India"] was sluggish this week as prices rebounded, while trading in top consumer China was subdued during the holiday-truncated trading period. Among other metals, spot silver gained 2.4% to $60.80 per ounce. Platinum jumped 3.6% to $1,692.85 and palladium climbed 2.5% to $1,151.08, but both metals were headed for a weekly loss.

item.title: Oil eases, bringing some respite to stocks and battered bonds
item.description: World stocks rose on Friday and oil prices slipped after US President Donald Trump said the US would not attackIran before next month's midterm elections, easing some near-term concerns about energy supplies.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Delevingne, Dhara Ranasinghe
item.content:encoded: World stocks rose on Friday and oil prices slipped after US President Donald Trump said the US would [USN:L1N45V03A TEXT:"not attack"] Iran before next month's midterm elections , easing some near-term concerns about energy supplies. Investors remained cautious, however, as they weighed another wave of fundraising by technology companies while borrowing costs in some of the world's biggest economies hovered near multi-year highs. European shares (.STOXX) gained 1.25% and Wall Street stocks were [USN:L4N45V10C TEXT:"positive"] too, with the S&P 500 (.SPX) ticking up 0.33% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) rising 0.4%. Brent crude futures fell about 0.75% to $103 per barrel after surging more than 4% in the previous session. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) rose 0.56%, while Japan's Nikkei (.N225) closed little changed on the day. The third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week with a number of [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"Wall Street banks set to report"]. Doug Beath, global equity strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute, said that relatively narrow market participation in the S&P 500 suggests investors believe large technology stocks are better positioned to withstand higher oil prices and rising yields, while remaining cautious about other areas of the market. "A disappointment, particularly in the tech sector, could trigger a pullback, and not just the usual choppy market we've come to expect," he added in an email. BONDS IN FOCUS US Treasury yields ticked up , after falling on Thursday, when a sale of 30-year government bonds drew solid demand. In Europe , government borrowing costs were broadly lower after a sharp selloff driven most recently by worries about high inflation and France's fiscal outlook. The premium investors demand to hold 10-year French debt over German Bunds was trading at about 137 basis points, and was on track to narrow by around 3 bps over the week . France has been hit particularly hard by the [USN:L6N45S11R TEXT:"global bond selloff"] as investors scrutinise its debt burden, budget deficit and political outlook ahead of the 2027 presidential election. "We are in a period following the central bank policy meetings and before earnings season, which means that markets are more vulnerable to being whiplashed by day-to-day commentary," said Guy Miller, chief market strategist at Zurich Insurance Group. CHIPS Chip stocks remained in focus after coming under pressure on Thursday on concerns about OpenAI. Reuters reported that the ChatGPT owner told investors its annualised [USN:L6N45U1FJ TEXT:"September"] revenue was almost $50 billion, below earlier signals, although Bloomberg reported the firm could reach or exceed $70 billion by year-end. "Investors are becoming more discriminating about AI valuations while renewed demand for government bonds is emerging at elevated yields," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro at Lombard Odier. Investors were also assessing a fresh wave of fundraising, with SpaceX (SPCX.O) , Broadcom (AVGO.O) and Oracle (ORCL.N) all expected to raise billions of dollars to buy advanced AI chips. Australian data centre operator Firmus, backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , shelved its $5-billion [USN:L1N45U12T TEXT:"initial public offering"], citing market volatility, and said it would pursue a private fundraising round instead. A combination of higher energy costs, expectations of further central bank interest-rate hikes and concerns about rising government debt has fuelled a months-long global bond selloff, pushing borrowing costs higher. "With long-term yields back around multi-decade highs, investors no longer have the luxury of valuing AI growth in a low-cost-of-capital world," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. Higher sovereign yields and rising corporate debt issuance to fund AI infrastructure mean capital is becoming "both more expensive and more selective, which puts balance sheets and the quality of future earnings firmly in focus," Chanana said. In currency markets, the dollar stood tall as the euro headed for a fifth consecutive weekly decline, trading at $1.119 and near the 17-month low touched earlier this week amid concerns over French debt. Gold [USN:L1N45V050 TEXT:"rose more than 1%"] to around $4,189 an ounce, helped by a slightly softer US dollar and lower oil prices.

item.title: Hurricane Isaias strengthens as US Gulf Coast prepares for landfall
item.description: Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding.
item.dc:creator: Brad Brooks
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Isaias strengthened on Thursday as it barreled toward the US Gulf Coast, prompting mandatory evacuations in parts of Florida and emergency declarations in Alabama as forecasters warned of life-threatening storm surges, tornadoes and flooding. Isaias has already severely disrupted oil and gas production in the Gulf of Mexico, forcing energy companies to evacuate offshore platforms and shut down operations. The first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season was packing maximum sustained winds of 85 mph (140 kph) early on Thursday, the US National Hurricane Center said. Isaias was forecast to strengthen to near Category 3 intensity, with sustained winds reaching 110 mph (175 kph) on Friday before reaching the northern Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday. "We are expecting Isaias to be a dangerous hurricane when it makes landfall,” NHC director Michael Brennan said in a Thursday morning briefing. "Today is the day to prepare and get ready." Isaias nearly tied the record for the latest first Atlantic hurricane with one that hit on October 8, 1905. The strong El Nino weather pattern this year has suppressed Atlantic hurricane development by increasing vertical wind shear, which disrupts the formation of strengthening tropical storms. The hurricane was moving east-northeast at 10 mph (17 kph), about 355 miles (570 km) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River at 1 p.m. US Central time, the NHC said. IMPACTS ON OIL, GAS The Marine Minerals Administration, which monitors offshore US oil and gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico, said on Thursday that personnel have been evacuated from 121 production platforms and five non-dynamically positioned rigs ahead of the storm. About 63% of current oil production in the Gulf, or 1.3 million barrels of oil a day, has been shut in, the agency said, citing operator reports. Just over 1.1 billion cubic feet a day of natural gas production has also been shut in, or about 57% of total output from the region. On Wednesday, 25% of oil production and 16% of natural gas output had been shut in. About 9 million barrels of oil production could be lost across the Gulf through the duration of the storm, a marked increase from the 7.1 million barrels impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha in July, according to a model forecast from consulting firm Earth Science Associates. The companies with the most exposure to the storm include BP, Chevron (CVX.N) , ENI, Murphy Oil (MUR.N) and Shell (SHEL.L) , among others, according to the Earth Science model. WARNINGS, STORM SURGE Hurricane warnings stretched from coastal Mississippi through Alabama to the Florida panhandle, while tropical-storm and storm-surge warnings extended into southeastern Louisiana, the NHC said. Forecasters warned that storm surges could reach 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2.1 meters) above sea level in the hardest-hit coastal areas, with rainfall of 3 to 7 inches (8 to 18 cm) and isolated totals of 15 inches (38 cm). The hurricane was forecast to weaken somewhat as it approached land. Increasing vertical wind shear, which can disrupt a hurricane's circulation, was expected to limit its strength near landfall, though forecasters warned it would remain dangerous. EVACUATIONS ORDERED In Florida, officials ordered mandatory evacuations beginning at noon local time on Thursday for coastal areas of Okaloosa County. The county urged tourists to leave the area and announced plans to close three airports Thursday evening. Governor Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in 25 Florida counties earlier in the week. Alabama Governor Kay Ivey declared a state of emergency covering 40 counties, while officials on Dauphin Island issued an evacuation notice for the western portion of the barrier island beginning Thursday evening. Baldwin County, Alabama, encouraged residents of low-lying coastal areas to evacuate voluntarily and prepared emergency shelters. In Mississippi, Jackson County and the city of Gautier declared local emergencies as coastal communities prepared for flooding and power outages.

item.title: Trump administration freezes green cards for Microsoft, IT firms, probes universities
item.description: The US suspended Microsoft, major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe from a key green-card program while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: The US suspended Microsoft (MSFT.O) , major IT outsourcers and software maker Adobe (ADBE.O) from a key green-card program on Thursday while opening probes into nine top universities, widening a crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs. Since taking office, US President Donald Trump has pursued a broad effort to reduce the number of foreign-born people in the US and curtail their pathway to residence and citizenship. Thursday's twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. His comments came hours before Trump honored tech billionaires for their contributions to America, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. Nadella once held an H-1B visa, as did Elon Musk, who was also honored, while three of the other CEOs honored are immigrants. Nadella thanked Trump for the medal, saying in a post on X he would continue to advance technology and drive American prosperity. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, or the [USN:L4N45U1DA TEXT:"permanent labor certification"] process, according to data from the US labor department. Under PERM, which most employment-based green cards require, employers must show a foreign hire will not hurt US workers' wages or jobs. The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would [USN:L4N4380XC TEXT:"cut 4,800 jobs"], or about 2.1% of its global workforce. CRACKDOWN WIDENS Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said. He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data. Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," and that the administration wanted the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then point to the lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research. “It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent $40 billion a year while in the US, she said. The probe deepens the administration's [USN:L1N45M14M TEXT:"long-running fight"] with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires. Rapidly changing visa policies caused a sharp drop in international applications to Columbia University and contributed to the university pausing admissions to one of its journalism programs, Reuters reported last week.

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Wall Street vue en hausse, soulagement sur le pétrole et l'obligataire
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Wall Street vue en hausse, soulagement sur le pétrole et l'obligataire 9 octobre (Reuters) - Wall Street est attendue en hausse vendredi et les Bourses européennes amplifient leurs gains à mi-séance, l'apaisement concernant l'approvisionnement en hydrocarbures depuis le Moyen-Orient bénéficiant aux cours pétroliers comme au marché obligataire, tandis que les investisseurs restent attentifs à la situation budgétaire en France. La Chine et l'UE parviennent s'entendent sur les véhicules hybrides PÉKIN, 9 octobre (Reuters) - La Chine et l'Union européenne sont parvenues à un "accord" sur le commerce des véhicules hybrides, a annoncé vendredi le ministère chinois du Commerce, à l'issue de deux jours de négociations au cours desquelles l'UE a cherché à réduire son déficit commercial avec Pékin. Delta Air Lines abaisse ses prévisions de bénéfices, avec la hausse des coûts du carburant CHICAGO, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Delta Air Lines a réduit sa prévision de bénéfice annuel de près 25% vendredi, l'impact de la flambée des prix du carburant annulant à la fois la forte demande de voyages et la hausse des prix des billets. La BCE pourrait devoir procéder à de nouvelles hausses de taux, estime Dolenc La Banque centrale européenne (BCE) pourrait être contrainte de continuer à relever ses taux directeurs face au risque d'une aggravation de l'inflation mais le moment et l'ampleur d'une telle mesure restent bien trop incertains pour pouvoir être prédits, a déclaré Primož Dolenc, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la banque centrale slovène. Le secteur du luxe freiné davantage par des mesures fiscales en Chine PARIS/PEKIN, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Le tour de vis enclenché par la Chine pour lutter contre l'évasion fiscale des plus fortunés est devenu un motif supplémentaire d'inquiétude pour les enseignes de luxe, lesquelles font déjà face aux répercussions de la guerre en Iran et à un ralentissement de la consommation aux Etats-Unis. Le gouvernement allemand relève ses prévisions de croissance pour 2026 et 2027 Le gouvernement allemand a revu à la hausse ses prévisions économiques pour cette année et l'année prochaine, la guerre en Iran n'ayant pas un impact aussi sévère qu'initialement redouté, a déclaré jeudi le ministère de l'Economie. Zone euro: Les rendements obligataires se tendent encore Les rendements obligataires de la zone euro enregistrent jeudi de nouvelles fortes tensions, dans un contexte de hausse des prix de l'énergie, les investisseurs continuant à se débarrasser des obligations des pays les plus endettés comme la France et l'Italie, provoquant un creusement des "spreads" dans le bloc. Aux yeux du patron de Ryanair, le coût du kérosène restera élevé une année de plus Les compagnies aériennes européennes vont connaître une nouvelle année de coûts de carburant élevés et de taris en hausse, la guerre en Iran maintenant les prix du kérosène à un niveau supérieur d'environ 50% à celui d'avant le conflit, a déclaré jeudi Michael O'Leary, directeur général de Ryanair. Le choc géopolitique se répercute désormais sur les marchés financiers, selon Moulin (BCE) La quasi-totalité du choc inflationniste subi par l'Europe cette année est liée à l'énergie, mais les chocs géopolitiques à l'origine de la flambée des prix "se traduisent désormais par un choc financier", a déclaré jeudi Emmanuel Moulin, gouverneur de la Banque de France (BdF) et membre de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE). BCE-Wunsch contre un relèvement du ratio de réserves obligatoires des banques La projet de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE) visant à relever le ratio de réserves obligatoires imposé aux banques commerciales pourrait nuire à la crédibilité de ses futures opérations, voire empiéter sur la politique budgétaire des Etats, a déclaré jeudi Pierre Wunsch, membre du Conseil des gouverneurs de l'institution de Francfort et gouverneur de la Banque nationale de Belgique.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les deux Renoir dérobés au musée de Cagnes-sur-Mer retrouvés PARIS, 9 octobre (Reuters) - Les deux tableaux dérobés il y a un peu plus d'un mois au musée Renoir de Cagnes-sur-Mer (Alpes-Maritimes) ont été retrouvés par la police et six suspects ont été arrêtés, a déclaré vendredi le maire Rassemblement national (RN) de la ville, Bryan Masson. Nobel/Littérature: Le prix décerné à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson Le prix Nobel de littérature a été décerné jeudi à la poète et écrivaine canadienne Anne Carson pour "son oeuvre audacieuse et inventive qui, dans un dialogue ludique avec la tradition classique, a créé de nouvelles formes pour la littérature contemporaine", a annoncé jeudi l'Académie royale des sciences de Suède. L'Allemagne abandonne le projet de char commun avec la France-Mandon PARIS, 8 octobre (Reuters) - L'Allemagne a décidé d'abandonner le projet avec la France de char commun du futur, le MGCS ("Main Ground Combat System", système principal de combat terrestre), a annoncé jeudi le chef d'état-major des armées, Fabien Mandon, lors d'une audition devant une commission parlementaire. France-Dix millions de barils de gazole libérés des réserves pour baisser les prix à la pompe-Lecornu La France va libérer 10 millions de barils de gazole de ses réserves stratégiques avec l'objectif d'agir sur les prix à la pompe, qui devraient ainsi "mécaniquement baisser" de 12 centimes à 18 centimes d'euro par litre de gazole, a déclaré mercredi soir le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu. Le Danemark accuse la Russie d'actes de sabotage contre ses entreprises du secteur de la défense La Russie a lancé des opérations de sabotage contre des entreprises danoises fournissant l'Ukraine après avoir conclu que ses tentatives de perturbation à plus grande échelle n'avaient pas freiné le soutien militaire occidental à Kyiv, a déclaré mercredi une responsable des services de renseignement danois. Nuñez suspend l'usage des grenades assourdissantes contre les lycéens L'usage des grenades assourdissantes par les forces de l'ordre est suspendu "dans le cadre du mouvement lycéen", a annoncé mercredi sur RTL le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez. De plus en plus d'enfants non accompagnés empruntent des voies dangereuses pour rejoindre l'Europe, selon l'Onu Plus des deux tiers des enfants réfugiés et migrants qui ont rejoint l'Europe par les routes de la Méditerranée et des Balkans en 2025 étaient non accompagnés et bon nombre d'entre eux ont été victimes d'exploitation, selon un rapport publié mercredi par des agences des Nations Unies. La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur sur ses finances publiques dit Citadel La France ne peut plus se permettre la moindre erreur dans l'assainissement de ses finances publiques et la pression exercée par les marchés devrait inciter le gouvernement à se concentrer sur la maîtrise des dépenses à l'approche de l'élection présidentielle de 2027, a déclaré à Reuters Angel Ubide, économiste chez la société de gestion d'actifs Citadel. Nobel/Chimie-Le Français Henri Kagan et le Japonais Kenso Soai distingués pour avoir résolu le mystère des molécules "images miroir" Le prix Nobel de chimie a été décerné mercredi à Henri Kagan et à Kenso Soai pour avoir résolu une énigme de longue date sur la manière de former une seule des deux "images miroir" d'une molécule, une découverte d'une grande importance pour la fabrication de médicaments, a annoncé mercredi l'Académie royale des sciences de Suède. États-Unis: Christa Pike est consciente et capable de parler selon ses avocats Christa Pike, dont l'exécution a échoué la semaine dernière dans le Tennessee, a repris conscience et retrouvé l'usage de la parole, ont déclaré ses avocats dans un communiqué publié mardi soir.
